Figure 1: Study setup inspired by Alshahwan et al. [5]: We first prompt the LLM to generate new tests given an existing test file.
Then, the generated code is added to the existing test file before compilation. After compilation, we identify the newly added,
generated tests, execute them in separate Docker containers, and store the results in a database.

   Motivation: Previous work on LLM-based test generation found             1   statement ok
                                                                            2   CREATE TABLE test (a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
that when generating new tests, LLMs follow existing coding con-            3   statement ok
ventions and adhere to the structure of the code presented in the           4   INSERT INTO test VALUES (11, 1), (12, 2), (13, 3);
                                                                            5   statement ok
context of a prompt [5, 37]. Harman et al. [36] called this effect          6   CREATE TABLE test2 (b INTEGER, c INTEGER);
“Fashion Following” and argued that the resulting test code is thus         7   statement ok
                                                                            8   INSERT INTO test2 VALUES (1, 10), (1, 20), (2, 30);
more intuitive to human readers. This “Fashion Following” can be            9   # simple cross product + join condition
                                                                           10   query III
attributed to the ability of LLM to learn from examples in the given       11   SELECT a, test.b, c FROM test, test2 WHERE test.b = test2.b ORDER BY c;
input context, that is, in-context learning (ICL) [17, 73]. ICL has        12   ----
                                                                           13   11      1       10
been shown to be an effective approach to improve the performance          14   11      1       20
of an LLM on various tasks [17]. However, previous research has            15   12      2       30

also shown that LLMs lack robustness against spurious correlations                  Listing 1: Example structure of an SQL test for DuckDB.
when learning from the provided context [38, 67]. We hypothesized
that, for test amplification, this may lead to the transfer of flakiness
from the existing tests, which are shown to the LLM, to the newly
                                                                                Table 2: An overview of the relevant existing tests in our
generated test code. Therefore, we aimed to gain insights into the
                                                                                study subjects.
robustness of LLMs against such a flakiness transfer.
   Approach: We injected flakiness into existing tests and repli-
cated our test generation experiment with the injected flaky tests.                   Metric           SAP HANA          MySQL       SQLite     DuckDB
More specifically, we added an assertion to the C++ tests that fails                  #Tests                 19 947          2127    388 282      236 185
with 50% probability, using the following steps [21]: (1) Parse the                   #Flaky Tests       13 (0.07%)    13 (0.61%)          0            0
original code of the given tests from the C++ files. (2) Add an asser-
tion to the test, which may fail based on the outcome of a coin flip
at the end of the test code. (3) Replace the original test code with
the injected code for every test in all relevant test files. (4) Persist        and repeated the injection experiments two additional times to en-
the injected files for later use. We performed these steps before               sure the reported proportion of tests containing the flaky assertion
providing the test files to the LLM and evaluated whether the LLM               is valid. Furthermore, in all our experiments, we set the tempera-
“follows” the injected flakiness in its generated output.                       ture to zero, as this setting has been shown to promise the most
                                                                                consistent results in a previous study [57].

   On the Impact of Flakiness Injection. Overall, we observe                            Our findings substantiate the importance of providing LLMs
that the LLM transfers the injected flaky assertion to a notable                     with appropriate context when employing them for test generation.
number of newly generated tests for both study subjects. Since                       We motivate practitioners to pay attention not only to engineering
the flaky assertion in the provided context is clearly not causally                  goals such as coverage or mutation scores when evaluating LLMs
related to the task at hand, we attribute this finding to the LLM’s                  for test generation, but also to consider potential side effects of the
susceptibility to spurious correlations in in-context learning. We                   resulting tests, such as flakiness. We encourage future studies to
conjecture that the LLM overvalues the provided context compared                     evaluate and extend our test generation setup by including addi-
to the knowledge gained from pre-training. While this may lead to                    tional test generation approaches and models. We also encourage
desirable effects such as the “Fashion Following” of existing coding                 researchers to investigate the impact of shortcut learning on the
conventions [36], the results of our simple setup suggest that this                  application of LLMs for automating software engineering tasks.
happens without any semantic understanding of the given code,
which may also lead to undesired properties in code synthesized by
LLM in practice. Therefore, we encourage future work to investigate
this effect. For example, future studies could further validate the                  References
